extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in the book A Glimpse of Hell, the USS Iowa turret explosion, or investigative journalism around military incidents
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic entry summarizing the nonfiction investigative journalism book A Glimpse of Hell, including background, content summary, reception, legal aftermath, and sources used by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative journalism quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluated by information gathering, accuracy of main outlines, and readability (gripping narrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes quoted on the page: 'In its main outlines, it convinces' and 'Measured by its information gathering, this is a great book of investigative journalism.' Another review said the book 'provides a gripping read.' These remarks imply criteria of thorough research, accuracy in key claims, and compelling storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sources and methods (journalistic thoroughness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment based on the author's methods: interviews with ex-military personnel and crew, assistance from former officers, Freedom of Information Act requests, depositions, and committee staff help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes Thompson's use of: ex-military officers (e.g., Ed Snyder), Iowa crewmembers, family members, House and Senate Armed Services Committee staff, FOIA requests, and depositions taken during lawsuits. These are presented as the factual and methodological basis supporting the book's conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on primary documents and independent technical review
rubrics_metrics.description: Strength of claims judged by use of primary evidence and corroboration by independent technical analysis (e.g., Sandia National Laboratories review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sandia's independent review (requested by the Senate Armed Services Committee) concluded an overram was probable, contrasting with the Navy's initial finding. The page highlights the role of independent technical analysis in overturning or challenging official investigative conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and scene-preservation as investigative standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper investigative procedure includes photographing and recording body/equipment locations at an accident scene; failure to do so undermines investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book alleges that after the fires were contained, the crew cleaned up and removed bodies and equipment 'all without photographing or otherwise recording the locations of the bodies or equipment which would have presumably assisted with the resulting investigation.' This omission is presented as a flaw in the Navy's handling and a criterion for evaluating the quality of an investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and conflict-of-interest in official investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Credibility of an investigation depends on absence of conflicts of interest and absence of external interference by senior officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites claims that Captain Joseph Miceli supervised preparation of powder and shells (creating a conflict if those items were investigated), and that Admiral Leon A. Edney 'interfered with the investigation' by sending suggestions and pushing for a particular finding. These are presented as factors that weaken official investigative findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of investigatory focus / burden of proof for intentionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations of deliberate acts require strong evidence; premature or weakly supported allegations (e.g., accusing a deceased sailor of intentional wrongdoing) are problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milligan's investigation concluded the explosion was 'most probably' an intentional act by Clayton Hartwig; critics (press, families, Congress) and subsequent analysis argued the evidence against the sailor was very weak ('guilt by fiat'). This illustrates the standard that findings of intentional wrongdoing need robust supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal vulnerability of publishing disputed factual claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Books making allegations about individuals or organizations risk suits for libel, false light privacy, and conspiracy if plaintiffs claim defamatory or false portrayals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recounts that in 2001 five Navy servicemen named in the book sued Thompson, the publisher, and a source for libel, false light privacy, and conspiracy; suits were later settled. The article also notes jurisdictional rulings (South Carolina long-arm jurisdiction) and that the publisher did not publicly retract the material but sent a letter expressing regret for emotional distress—indicating legal and reputational consequences to consider when producing such work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution and institutional pushback as measure of controversy/impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The reception and institutional response (e.g., bans from Navy exchanges, rescinded speaking invitations) indicate perceived controversy and impact of a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thompson claimed the Navy 'banned the book from Navy exchange stores' and rescinded a speaking invitation; the Navy denied suppression but refused permission for base book signings. Salon.com checks reportedly did not find the book for sale at certain Navy locations. These distribution issues are presented as indicators of the book's contentious reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public and commercial reception metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection for clubs, TV adaptation, Nielsen ratings, and sales rankings are metrics for a book's reach and mainstream reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book was selected by the Book of the Month Club, adapted into an FX TV movie that drew 2.7 million viewers and high ratings for the network, and had an Amazon sales ranking (noted at #997,726 overall and No. 85 in State of Iowa books as of a cited date). Such metrics are used on the page to indicate the book's public reach and commercial performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity with official investigative procedural rules (JAGMAN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations conducted under Navy legal/procedural frameworks (e.g., JAGMAN one-officer investigation) are governed by specified rules and procedures which affect admissibility and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The references note that the 'one-officer investigation' was often referred to as a 'JAGMAN' and that its rules and procedures were laid out in the Navy's Manual of the Judge Advocate General, Chapter 5, Part C. This highlights that official investigative format and procedure are standards to evaluate the legitimacy of inquiry outcomes.
